title: A failed NPC reply is also a game-state decision
author: Comfortable-Cat-9611
selftext:
I made The Interview, a small Unity interrogation game where players write their own questions. The language model supplies the character's words; C# owns the case file, composure, question budget and final clearance choice. One problem that deserves its own design decision is what happens when a reply never arrives.



Disclosure: the free game uses my own paid Unity tool, Offline AI NPC. The point here is the recovery behaviour, which also applies to a custom implementation.



Three different outcomes



A coherent answer, a contradictory answer and a backend failure should not be treated as the same event. A contradictory answer is still a generated line. In the current game, it is not automatically caught by a semantic fact checker. Keeping the case and verdict mechanics in code does not prove that every sentence agrees with the dossier.



The recovery path described here is narrower: the dialogue turn fails and produces no spoken answer. This is separate from deciding whether the model understood the question or whether its answer was truthful.



What the player gets back



The game permits eighteen questions. When that failure path is taken, the submitted question is removed from the repeat-question history and the used-question counter is reduced by one. If the question had exhausted the budget, that end condition is cleared so the player can try again.



However, the pressure already applied by the chosen approach remains. This is a partial recovery, not a complete rollback. Pressing or accusing a character has already changed the scene's composure state. Restoring a question does not restore every consequence of asking it.



This distinction matters to the explanation shown to players. Calling the question 'refunded' without specifying the resource makes it sound as if composure, inference tokens or the entire turn state has been reset. The actual promise is much smaller: the missing answer does not also use up one of the limited questions.



Words still matter during failure



The failure path has an authored line about the connection dropping briefly and asking again. That gives the interface a visible response instead of leaving an empty answer. It still interrupts the fiction, particularly if the player interprets the silence as evidence about the character.



An in-character request to repeat the question could be less disruptive, but it also risks hiding a technical failure inside the conversation. A repeated canned answer can become conspicuous. These are design trade-offs; I have not run a comparison study proving that one is better.



Recovery and truth are separate checks



A fallback for a missing reply does not protect a mystery from plausible invented details. A semantic check against the case would need its own rules for contradiction, acceptable uncertainty and replacement dialogue. That is an idea worth evaluating, not a capability I claim for the current demo.



Likewise, the question cap changes the cost of a turn, but I have not measured whether it makes model mistakes more noticeable. It is a constraint in the game, not evidence about every player's experience.



The behaviour above was checked by reading the session and scene recovery code; it is not a new runtime benchmark. My next design question is about the experience that code creates: after a backend failure, would you preserve the player's pressure choice, restore the entire turn, or make retrying an explicit separate action?



Context: the free Windows game is at [https://merrymaker14.itch.io/the-interview](https://merrymaker14.itch.io/the-interview) . The attached image is a real gameplay capture for context, not a capture of this failure path.



Writing and translation were AI-assisted; the described behaviour was checked against the game code.
